Traditional Mushroom Ketchup

British · Medium · Makes about 350 ml

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The oldest ketchup on the English table — older than the tomato version by a century and the reason the word "ketchup" exists at all. This is the eighteenth-century original: mushrooms packed in salt until they weep their own dark liquid, that liquid simmered with spice, bottled into a thin, intensely savoury sauce the colour of strong tea. It is not red, it is not sweet, and it tastes of nothing but mushroom, concentrated to its absolute limit. A few dashes in gravy, a spoonful over the grilled breakfast tomatoes, a splash in the pan after the sausages come out — this is the café cook's secret weapon, and it was the country's most popular sauce before the tomato stole the name. The method is a two-stage extraction, and it could not be more honest: salt draws the liquid out overnight, heat and time finish the job. No vinegar, no sugar — just mushrooms, salt, and spice. The result keeps for months in the fridge because salt is the preservative.

- **Slice or leave whole — both work.** Sliced mushrooms salt faster and yield by morning; whole ones take a few hours longer. Either way, the salt does the work, not the knife. - **Choose a non-reactive vessel** for the overnight cure — glass, ceramic, or stainless. Aluminium and unlined copper react with the salt and taint the liquor. - **The 3% salt rule:** weigh the mushrooms, multiply by 0.03, and measure that salt. At 1 kg it is 30 g. This is the recipe's preservative backbone; a lighter hand gives you a sauce that spoils rather than keeps. - Set a clean 350 ml bottle or jar to sterilise: 10 minutes in a 140 °C oven, lid in boiling water.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • Overnight cure: 300 ml+ dark liquid, fully collapsed mushrooms.
  • Hot extraction: clear mahogany liquor, never boiled, aromatics spent.
  • Reduction: light spoon-coat, intense savoury-salt balance, nutmeg warmth.
  • Bottled hot; kept cold; clear and still after a week.

Traditional Mushroom Ketchup

Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 1 hour, plus overnight salt rest · Total: Overnight plus 1½ hours · Makes about 350 ml

Ingredients

The mushrooms

  • 1 kg cultivated button or chestnut mushrooms (a 250 g addition of wild mushrooms — field, portobello trimmings, or dried porcini, 15 g, soaked — deepens it further)

The salt cure

  • 30 g fine sea salt (3% of mushroom weight — this is a preserve, not a seasoning)

The aromatics, for simmering

  • 2 shallots (60 g), quartered
  • ½ nutmeg, grated (about 1 g), or a whole half simmered and lifted
  • 6 black peppercorns
  • 1 bay leaf
  • 1 strip orange zest or 2 g ground allspice (the older recipes split between the two)
  • 1 clove garlic, crushed
  • 75 ml water (only if the mushrooms yield less liquid than needed)

To finish and stabilise

  • 30 ml sherry vinegar or cider vinegar (optional — the pure Victorian version omits it; the vinegar guarantees keeping)
  • 15 ml dry sherry or Madeira (optional, and excellent)

Instructions

  1. **The overnight cure.** Layer the mushrooms with the salt in your ceramic or glass bowl, pressing them down so the layers contact. Cover with a cloth and leave 12–18 hours at cool room temperature. By morning the salt has pulled a surprising depth of dark liquid from the mushrooms, which will have collapsed to about half their volume. Checkpoint — the bowl holds at least 300 ml of dark, tea-coloured liquid and the mushrooms have slumped and look thoroughly deflated. If the yield looks thin, stir gently, give it another 4 hours — the salt is still working.
  2. **The hot extraction.** Tip the mushrooms and every drop of their liquid into a stainless pan. Add the shallots, nutmeg, peppercorns, bay, orange zest or allspice, and garlic. Set over the lowest heat and bring to the barest tremor — not a boil. Hold it there, uncovered, 45 minutes, pressing the mushrooms against the pan's side with a spoon every 10 minutes to squeeze out the last of their liquor. Checkpoint — the liquid has darkened further to deep mahogany, the mushrooms have gone grey-brown and lifeless (their flavour is now in the liquid, where it belongs), and the surface carries only the occasional slow bubble.
  3. **Strain without pressing.** Set a fine sieve or a colander lined with muslin over a clean pan and pour everything through. Let the mushrooms drain by gravity for 10 minutes, pressing only very gently at the end. You want the clear, dark liquor; hard squeezing pushes through cloudiness and sediment. Checkpoint — the strained liquor runs clear and dark — translucent mahogany held to the light — with no flecks or murk.
  4. **Reduce to ketchup strength.** Simmer the strained liquor over medium-low heat 10–20 minutes until it reduces by about a third and the flavour concentrates to an intense, salty-savoury depth. Add the vinegar and sherry if using, and simmer 2 minutes more. Taste with the tip of a spoon — it should be assertively salty, deeply mushroomy, and warming with nutmeg. Checkpoint — the sauce coats a spoon lightly — thinner than tomato ketchup, thicker than water — and a single drop on the tongue is a full, savoury statement. This is a seasoning sauce; intensity is the point.
  5. **Bottle hot.** Pour through a funnel into the sterilised bottle, seal, cool, and refrigerate. The sauce keeps 3 months cold and improves for the first two weeks as the spice rounds into the mushroom. Checkpoint — after a week, the flavour has married — no sharp salt edge, just depth. The bottle, well handled (clean spoon, refrigerated), shows no fizz or cloudiness.

Finish & Plate

Use it in dashes and spoonfuls, rarely at the table straight: a few drops into the pan gravy for bangers, a spoonful stirred into the vegetarian full English's beans, a splash in the frying pan swirled into the bacon's rendered fat to make an instant sauce for the fried eggs. The old café trick is a teaspoon of mushroom ketchup in a mug of strong builder's tea for a beef-tea-like revival — historical, if not for everyone. Bottles of this make the best kind of gift: cheap to make, impossible to buy.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Mushrooms yielded little liquid overnightToo little salt, or cured too brieflyWeigh the salt at 3%; stir and extend the cure 4 hours
Cloudy sauceBoiled hard, or mushrooms squeezed in the strainerLowest heat only; drain by gravity, press gently at most
Too salty to use even in dashesSalt ratio drifted high25 ml water + 5 minutes' re-simmer; use in cooking rather than at table
Fermented smell or fizz in the bottleUnder-salted, under-refrigerated, or contaminated handlingDiscard; next batch: full 3% salt, vinegar added, clean spoon always
Weak mushroom flavourSupermarket white mushrooms onlyAdd 15 g dried porcini (soaked) or 250 g chestnut/wild to the cure

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Storage:** refrigerated 3 months with the vinegar, 4–6 weeks without. The Victorian version, bottled hot and kept in a cool larder, was used over a similar span — but the fridge is the modern guarantee. - **Variation — double-extraction (the deep version):** after straining, return the spent mushrooms to the pan with 150 ml just-boiled water, simmer 20 minutes, and strain this second, weaker liquor into the first before reducing. It stretches the yield and captures the last of the flavour. - **Variation — walnut ketchup (the sibling):** the same method with 1 kg young green walnuts in June — the other great English ketchup, jet black and unforgettably bold. - **The batch cook:** a kilogram of mushrooms makes a month of flavouring for a household — one Sunday afternoon, four weeks of gravies.
